component.name: Apache Kvrocks
component.description: Distributed key-value NoSQL database using RocksDB as its storage engine, compatible with the Redis (RESP) protocol, adding namespace-token multi-tenancy, binlog-based async replication, Redis-Sentinel failover, and a proxyless centralized cluster mode. Clients speak RESP over TCP (default port 6666, default bind 127.0.0.1); the requirepass value is the admin token, and each namespace is gated by its own token.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it. The source is a v0 draft by the ASF Security team, reviewed by the Kvrocks PMC (PragmaTwice) with all open questions resolved.

blueprints.name: Kvrocks server deployment
blueprints.description: The trust boundary is the TCP connection plus the token presented on it: a connection's identity (unauthenticated, namespace, admin) determines which commands and which keyspace it may touch. Replication ships a binlog from master to replica; replication and cluster peers are operator-provisioned and trusted.

assets.name: Kvrocks server (RESP command layer)
assets.description: TCP listener, RESP command dispatch, authentication and namespace isolation, and the admin command surface (config, slaveof, bgsave, namespace, cluster, debug).

assets.name: Lua scripting sandbox
assets.description: EVAL/FUNCTION scripts execute in the embedded LuaJIT sandbox, confined to the caller's namespace with no host access.

assets.name: RocksDB storage
assets.description: All namespaces share one RocksDB instance on local disk; data at rest is not encrypted by Kvrocks and no per-namespace encryption is claimed.

assets.name: Replication and cluster channel
assets.description: Binlog stream from master to replica and proxyless cluster coordination (slot migration); peers are mutually trusted within the topology.

zones.name: TCP clients
zones.description: Redis-protocol clients: unauthenticated until a valid token is presented, then confined to a namespace or granted admin control.

zones.name: Kvrocks server process
zones.description: The server, its Lua sandbox, and its RocksDB data directory on an operator-trusted host.

zones.name: Replication and cluster peers
zones.description: Other Kvrocks nodes in the same topology, operator-provisioned on a trusted network; trusted, so a malicious peer is out of the adversary model.

persona.description: A TCP peer that has not presented a valid token; untrusted. With tokens configured, commands beyond AUTH are refused.

Authenticated with a namespace token; trusted only within that namespace's keyspace and denied admin/namespace/cluster commands. The namespace token is a shared per-namespace secret, not a per-user credential.
Authenticated with the requirepass admin token; trusted for the instance. requirepass is the admin token, root-equivalent, not a low-privilege password.
Controls kvrocks.conf, the data directory, TLS material, and network exposure; fully trusted, out of model as an adversary.

assumptions.description: A POSIX host with a trusted local filesystem for the RocksDB data directory; the operator controls who can reach the listening port, and the default bind 127.0.0.1 limits exposure to localhost until changed.
Replication and cluster peers are provisioned by the operator on a trusted network.

The server binds a TCP port, reads/writes its data directory and kvrocks.conf, opens outbound connections to masters/peers, and may write RDB/backup files on bgsave; it is not assumed to spawn shells or read arbitrary files outside its data dir (Lua sandbox permitting).

threats.name: Cross-namespace read or write by a namespace client
threats.description: A connection authenticated with a namespace token accesses another namespace's keyspace or namespace metadata (which is admin-only). Strict per-namespace keyspace confinement is a claimed, PMC-confirmed property; a bypass (excluding the documented pub/sub limitation) is critical. Isolation is logical, not cryptographic: all namespaces share one RocksDB instance.

threats.name: Admin command executed without the admin token
threats.description: A namespace-authenticated or unauthenticated client runs a sensitive admin command (config, slaveof, bgsave, namespace management, cluster operations) that only the requirepass admin token may run. Critical.

threats.name: Pre-authentication data access
threats.description: With requirepass or namespace tokens configured, commands beyond AUTH must be refused on an unauthenticated connection; pre-auth data access is critical.

threats.name: Lua sandbox escape
threats.description: A script permitted to a non-admin caller breaks the LuaJIT sandbox to reach host resources or another namespace. Scripting is confined to the caller's namespace with no host or file access; an escape is critical.

threats.name: Memory corruption from crafted RESP input
threats.description: Well-formed or malformed RESP input causing out-of-bounds read/write or a crash from crafted input on supported platforms would violate the memory-safety property. Critical.

threats.name: Pub/sub channels cross namespaces (known limitation)
threats.description: Namespace keyspace confinement is strict for keys, but pub/sub channels are not currently namespaced: a namespace client can publish and subscribe across the instance. A documented current limitation rather than a property breach; a report matching exactly this behaviour is a known non-finding, and namespacing pub/sub is desirable hardening.

threats.name: Unauthenticated admin-level access when requirepass is unset
threats.description: requirepass ships unset (commented), so no authentication exists by default and all clients are effectively admin; the bind 127.0.0.1 default mitigates this until changed. When requirepass is unset, operators are responsible for restricting access to trusted personnel only; an unauthenticated-access report against a routable, no-requirepass deployment is operator responsibility.

threats.name: Token and data sniffing or MITM on an unencrypted wire
threats.description: TLS is opt-in (off by default); on an untrusted network the auth token and all data are observable and modifiable. As with requirepass, when TLS is off operators are responsible for restricting access to trusted personnel only.

threats.name: Resource exhaustion beyond configured limits
threats.description: Expensive commands (KEYS, large MGET, huge values, deep pipelines) and adversarial Lua can exhaust CPU/memory/disk; there is no intrinsic DoS guarantee beyond configured limits. The operator's contract is to configure maxclients and size limits; a hang/OOM/disk-fill is a property breach only if a configured limit is bypassed.

threats.name: Malicious replication or cluster peer
threats.description: A peer holding valid topology credentials that behaves maliciously is out of the adversary model: replication and cluster peers are operator-provisioned and trusted. Peer authenticity on the wire is a network/TLS concern for the operator.

threats.name: Non-constant-time AUTH token comparison
threats.description: A constant-time token compare in AUTH is desirable hardening, not a property breach; brute-force throttling is operator/network responsibility.

trustBoundaries.name: Client TCP trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Connect then AUTH: a new connection is unauthenticated and, once tokens are configured, commands are refused until a valid token is presented; a namespace token confines the connection to its keyspace, the admin token grants full control.

trustBoundaries.name: Replication and cluster trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The master streams a binlog to replicas which apply it; peers are mutually trusted within the topology, so this boundary is operator-provisioned trust, not an adversarial surface.

controls.name: Authentication gate on unauthenticated connections
controls.description: With requirepass or namespace tokens configured, commands beyond AUTH are refused on an unauthenticated connection.

controls.name: Strict per-namespace keyspace confinement
controls.description: A namespace-authenticated connection can access only that namespace's keyspace; namespace metadata is admin-only. Pub/sub is the one documented cross-namespace exception.

controls.name: Admin-token-only sensitive commands
controls.description: Only the requirepass admin token may run namespace management and sensitive admin commands (config, slaveof, bgsave, cluster operations); treat the admin token as root-equivalent, distribute only namespace tokens to tenants, and rotate on exposure.

controls.name: LuaJIT sandbox confinement
controls.description: EVAL/FUNCTION scripts run in a constrained LuaJIT environment without arbitrary host or file access, confined to the caller's namespace.

controls.name: Default bind 127.0.0.1
controls.description: The default bind of 127.0.0.1 limits exposure to localhost until the operator changes it; a safe default, so reports requiring a routable bind plus no auth are operator misconfiguration.

controls.name: Set requirepass and namespace tokens before non-localhost binding
controls.description: Set requirepass (and namespace tokens) before binding to any non-localhost interface; if requirepass is left unset, restrict access to trusted personnel only.

controls.name: Enable TLS on untrusted networks
controls.description: Enable TLS (tls-port, certificates, tls-auth-clients) on untrusted networks, or keep traffic on a trusted/segmented network; when TLS is off, restrict access to trusted personnel only.

controls.name: Configure resource limits
controls.description: Configure maxclients, value/proto size, and related limits for the deployment's risk profile; there is no intrinsic DoS guarantee beyond these.

controls.name: Run peers on a trusted network
controls.description: Run replication and cluster peers on a trusted network (and/or with TLS); peers are trusted, so the operator must provision them.

controls.name: Protect the data directory and backups
controls.description: Protect the RocksDB data directory and RDB/backup files at the filesystem layer; data at rest is not encrypted by Kvrocks and no per-namespace encryption is claimed.
